q-346167.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14223546/assets/2e8d832561b0dc49086f080feed8326b2098bc9986f3a6c298edbcf2662ae715.png)

For the function $f(x)=4x-{x}^{2}$ shown above, what is the expression for the area $A$ as a definite integral?

|  |  | {{field-1}} |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $A$ | $=$ | $\int $ | {{field-2}} | $\text{d}x$ |
|  |  | {{field-3}} |  |  |
q-346167.worked_solution:
We want to express the area $A$ between the function $f(x)=4x-{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis, between $x=2$ and $x=4.$

This can be expressed as the definite integral of $f(x)=4x-{x}^{2}$ between the lower limit $x=2$ and the upper limit $x=4,$ as follows:

$$
A={\int }_{2}^{4}4x-{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x
$$

For the function $f(x)=\frac{4x}{1+{x}^{2}}$ shown above, what is the expression for the area $A$ as a definite integral?
q-113878.worked_solution:
We want to express the area $A$ between the function $f(x)=\frac{4x}{1+{x}^{2}}$ and the $x$-axis, between $x=0$ and $x=3.$

This can be expressed as the definite integral of $f(x)=\frac{4x}{1+{x}^{2}}$ between the lower limit $x=0$ and the upper limit $x=3,$ as follows:

$$
A={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{4x}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x
$$

q-346162.worked_solution:
We want to express the area $A$ between the function $f(x)={x}^{2}+2$ and the $x$-axis, between $x=-2$ and $x=2.$

This can be expressed as the definite integral of $f(x)={x}^{2}+2$ between the lower limit $x=-2$ and the upper limit $x=2,$ as follows:

$$
A={\int }_{-2}^{2}{x}^{2}+2\,\text{d}x
$$

q-113868.html:
Question 4
?

For the function f(x)=x2−2x+2 shown above, what is the expression for the area A as a definite integral?

a
A=∫−30(−x2+2x−2)dx
b
A=∫−13(x2−2x+2)dx
c
A=∫03(x2−2x+2)dx
d
A=∫−30(x2−2x+2)dx
e
A=∫−10(−x2+2x−2)dx
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We want to express the area A between the function f(x)=x2−2x+2 and the x-axis, between x=0 and x=3.

This can be expressed as the definite integral of f(x)=x2−2x+2 between the lower limit x=0 and the upper limit x=3, as follows: A=∫03(x2−2x+2)dx

q-30382.name: Question 5
q-30382.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14223546/assets/e8a9dfb3ff189e96089c73ead8a3b44f04aa1684894c44203afb8884ad75c9e1.png)

For the function $f(x)=-{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2$ shown above, what is the expression for the area $A$ as a definite integral?
q-30382.worked_solution:
We want to express the area $A$ between the function $f(x)=-{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2$ and the $x$-axis, between $x=-1.5$ and $x=0.5.$

This can be expressed as the definite integral of $f(x)=-{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2$ between the lower limit $x=-1.5$ and the upper limit $x=0.5,$ as follows:

$$
A={\int }_{-1.5}^{0.5}(-{x}^{3}-{x}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}x
$$

q-30382.html:
Question 5
?

For the function f(x)=−x3−x2+2 shown above, what is the expression for the area A as a definite integral?

a
A=∫0−0.5(−x3−x2+2)dx
b
A=∫−1.50.5(−x3−x2)2dx
c
A=∫1.53(−x3−x2+2)dx
d
A=∫−1.50.5(−x3−x2+2)dx
e
A=∫1.53(−x3+2)2dx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We want to express the area A between the function f(x)=−x3−x2+2 and the x-axis, between x=−1.5 and x=0.5.

This can be expressed as the definite integral of f(x)=−x3−x2+2 between the lower limit x=−1.5 and the upper limit x=0.5, as follows:

A=∫−1.50.5(−x3−x2+2)dx

q-346169.name: Question 6
q-346169.problem:
Express ${\int }_{1}^{4}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x$ as the limit of a left Riemann sum.

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{1}^{4}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[3($
{{field-1}}
$)^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}]$
q-346169.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{4}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=3{x}^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=4.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{4-1}{n}=\frac{3}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}3{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[3{(\,1+\frac{3i}{n}\,)}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-346178.name: Question 7
q-346178.problem:
Express ${\int }_{1}^{7}\frac{2}{x+3}\,\text{d}x$ as the limit of a left Riemann sum.

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{1}^{7}\frac{2}{x+3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[($
{{field-1}}
$)\cdot \frac{6}{n}]$
q-346178.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{7}\frac{2}{x+3}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\frac{2}{x+3},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=7.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{7-1}{n}=\frac{6}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{7}\frac{2}{x+3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{6}{n})\cdot \frac{6}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{6i}{n})\cdot \frac{6}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\frac{2}{(1+6i/n)+3}\cdot \frac{6}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[(\frac{2}{6i/n+4})\cdot \frac{6}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[(\,\frac{1}{3i/n+2}\,)\cdot \frac{6}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-113884.name: Question 8
q-113884.problem: What is ${\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
q-113884.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={e}^{x-1},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-1}{n}=\frac{4}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{4}{n})\,\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{4i}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{1+4i/n-1}\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{4i/n}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-113884.html:
Question 8
?

What is ∫15ex−1dx expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑i=0n−1[e5i/n−1⋅5n]
b
limn→∞∑i=0n−1[e4i/n⋅4n]
c
limn→∞∑i=0n−1[e5i/n⋅4n]
d
limn→∞∑i=0n−1[e5i/n⋅5n]
e
limn→∞∑i=0n−1[e4i/n−1⋅4n]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as ∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1f(xi)⋅Δx,

where Δx=b−an and xi=a+iΔx.

In the definite integral ∫15ex−1dx, the function is f(x)=ex−1, the lower bound is a=1, and the upper bound is b=5. So, we have Δx=5−1n=4n,

and therefore ∫15ex−1dx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1f(xi)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[f(1+i⋅4n)⋅4n]=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[f(1+4in)⋅4n]=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[e1+4i/n−1⋅4n]=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[e4i/n⋅4n].

q-73155.name: Question 9
q-73155.problem: What is ${\int }_{2}^{5}2{x}^{1/3}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
q-73155.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{j}=a+jΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{2}^{5}2{x}^{1/3}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=2{x}^{1/3},$ the lower bound is $a=2,$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-2}{n}=\frac{3}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{5}2{x}^{1/3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{j})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[f(2+j\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[f(2+\frac{3j}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{j=0}^{n-1}[2{(2+\frac{3j}{n})}^{1/3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-73155.html:
Question 9
?

What is ∫252x1/3dx expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(2+3jn)1/3⋅3n]
b
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(2+3jn)⋅3n]
c
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(3jn)1/3⋅3n]
d
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[(3+3jn)1/3⋅3n]
e
limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(2+2jn)1/3⋅2n]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑j=0n−1f(xj)⋅Δx,

where Δx=b−an and xj=a+jΔx.

In the definite integral

∫252x1/3dx,

the function is f(x)=2x1/3, the lower bound is a=2, and the upper bound is b=5. So, we have

Δx=5−2n=3n,

and therefore

∫252x1/3dx=limn→∞∑j=0n−1f(xj)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑j=0n−1[f(2+j⋅3n)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑j=0n−1[f(2+3jn)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑j=0n−1[2(2+3jn)1/3⋅3n].

q-49189.name: Question 10
q-49189.problem: What is ${\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?
q-49189.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{l})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{l}=a+lΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={x}^{2},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{2-1}{n}=\frac{1}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{l})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[f(1+l\cdot \frac{1}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{l}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{l=0}^{n-1}[{(1+\frac{l}{n})}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-49189.html:
Question 10
?

What is ∫12x2dx expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?

a
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+2ln)2⋅1n]
b
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(2+ln)2⋅1n]
c
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+ln)2⋅1n]
d
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+2ln)2⋅2n]
e
 limn→∞∑l=0n−1[−(2+ln)2⋅2n]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑l=0n−1f(xl)⋅Δx,

where Δx=b−an and xl=a+lΔx.

In the definite integral

∫12x2dx,

the function is f(x)=x2, the lower bound is a=1, and the upper bound is b=2. So, we have Δx=2−1n=1n,

and therefore

∫12x2dx=limn→∞∑l=0n−1f(xl)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑l=0n−1[f(1+l⋅1n)⋅1n]=limn→∞∑l=0n−1[f(1+ln)⋅1n]=limn→∞∑l=0n−1[(1+ln)2⋅1n].
q-49189.knowledge_point: Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum

q-346190.name: Question 11
q-346190.problem:
Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that

$$
{\int }_{2}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[5{(2+\frac{4k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].
$$

$\,f(x)=$
{{field-1}} $\,$ and 
$\,b=$
{{field-2}}
q-346190.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=2.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{4}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{4}{n}=\frac{b-2}{n}\,⟹\,b=6.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=2+\frac{4k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=5{x}_{k}^{3}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{2}^{6}5{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[5{(2+\frac{4k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 

$$
f(x)=5{x}^{3}\,\text{and}\,b=6.
$$

q-346201.name: Question 12
q-346201.problem:
Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{((-1+\frac{3k}{n})+8)}^{1/3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].
$$

$\,f(x)=$
{{field-1}} $\,$ and 
$\,b=$
{{field-2}}
q-346201.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=-1.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{3}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{3}{n}=\frac{b-(-1)}{n}\,⟹\,b=2.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=-1+\frac{3k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=({x}_{k}+8)^{1/3}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{2}(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{((-1+\frac{3k}{n})+8)}^{1/3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 

$$
f(x)=(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{and}\,b=2.
$$

q-49235.name: Question 13
q-49235.problem: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that ${\int }_{e}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(e+\frac{ie}{n})\cdot \frac{e}{n}].$
q-49235.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=e.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{e}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{e}{n}=\frac{b-e}{n}\,⟹\,b=2e.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{i}=e+\frac{ie}{n}$ and $f({x}_{i})=\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}_{i}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{e}^{2e}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[\operatorname{ln}⁡(e+\frac{ie}{n})\cdot \frac{e}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x$ and $b=2e.$

Find the function f(x) and the value of b, given that ∫ebf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[ln⁡(e+ien)⋅en].

a
f(x)=ln⁡x and b=2e
b
f(x)=ln⁡(x+e) and b=e+1
c
f(x)=ln⁡(x+e) and b=2e
d
f(x)=ln⁡(x+e) and b=e2

f(x)=ln⁡x and b=e2

EXPLANATION

A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows: ∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1f(xi)⋅Δx where Δx=b−an and xi=a+iΔx.

Notice that we're given that the lower limit a=e.

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that Δx=en. Therefore, en=b−en⟹b=2e.

Consequently, xi=e+ien and f(xi)=ln⁡xi.

Hence, ∫e2eln⁡xdx=limn→∞∑i=0n−1[ln⁡(e+ien)⋅en].

Therefore, the correct answer is f(x)=ln⁡x and b=2e.

q-113918.name: Question 14
q-113918.problem: Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that ${\int }_{0}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{6i/n}\cdot \frac{6}{n}].$
q-113918.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=0.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{6}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{6}{n}=\frac{b-0}{n}\,⟹\,b=6.
$$

Consequently,  ${x}_{i}=\frac{6i}{n}$ and $f({x}_{i})={e}^{{x}_{i}}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{0}^{6}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{6i/n}\cdot \frac{6}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)={e}^{x}$ and $b=6.$

q-315828.problem:
Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that

$$
{\int }_{1}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{\,1+4k/n}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].
$$

$\,f(x)=$
{{field-1}} $\,$ and

q-315828.worked_solution:
A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=1.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{4}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{4}{n}=\frac{b-1}{n}\,⟹\,b=5.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=1+\frac{4k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})={e}^{\,{x}_{k}}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{\,1+4k/n}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 

$$
f(x)={e}^{x}\,\text{and}\,b=5.
$$

q-113929.name: Question 16
q-113929.problem: What is ${\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
q-113929.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{3}\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x,$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-0}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$

$$

q-113929.html:
Question 16
?

What is ∫03arctan⁡xdx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(kn)⋅1n]
b
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅1n]
c
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅3n]
d
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(k3n)⋅3n]
e
limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅13n]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as ∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx, where xk=a+kΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral ∫03arctan⁡xdx, the function is f(x)=arctan⁡x, the lower bound is a=0 and the upper bound is b=3. So, we have Δx=3−0n=3n.

Therefore, ∫03arctan⁡xdx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(0+k⋅3n)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(3kn)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[arctan⁡(3kn)⋅3n].

q-73180.name: Question 17
q-73180.problem: What is ${\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
q-73180.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=-2{x}^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=-2$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-(-2)}{n}=\frac{5}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(-2+k\cdot \frac{5}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(-2+\frac{5k}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[-2{(-2+\frac{5k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{5}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-73180.html:
Question 17
?

What is ∫−23−2x3dx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(2+kn)3⋅1n]
b
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(5+2kn)⋅2n]
c
limn→∞∑k=1n[−(−1+5kn)3⋅5n]
d
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(5kn)−2⋅5n]
e
limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(−2+5kn)3⋅5n]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx,

where xk=a+kΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral

∫−23−2x3dx,

the function is f(x)=−2x3, the lower bound is a=−2 and the upper bound is b=3. So, we have

Δx=3−(−2)n=5n.

Therefore,

∫−23−2x3dx=limn→∞∑k=1nf(xk)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(−2+k⋅5n)⋅5n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[f(−2+5kn)⋅5n]=limn→∞∑k=1n[−2(−2+5kn)3⋅5n].

q-346215.name: Question 18
q-346215.problem:
What is ${\int }_{1}^{4}(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{1}^{4}(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[($
{{field-1}}
$)^{1/3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}]$
q-346215.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{4}(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=(x+8)^{1/3},$ the lower bound is $a=1$ and the upper bound is $b=4.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{4-1}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{4}(x+8)^{1/3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(1+\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[{((1+\frac{3i}{n})+8)}^{1/3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[{(\,9+\frac{3i}{n}\,)}^{1/3}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=1nf(xi)⋅Δx,

where xi=a+iΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral

∫14(x+8)1/3dx,

the function is f(x)=(x+8)1/3, the lower bound is a=1 and the upper bound is b=4. So, we have

Δx=4−1n=3n.

Therefore,

∫14(x+8)1/3dx=limn→∞∑i=1nf(xi)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑i=1n[f(1+i⋅3n)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑i=1n[f(1+3in)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑i=1n[((1+3in)+8)1/3⋅3n]=limn→∞∑i=1n[(9+3in)1/3⋅3n].

q-73181.name: Question 19
q-73181.problem: What is ${\int }_{-4}^{-1}\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4}\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
q-73181.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{-1}\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4},$ the lower bound is $a=-4$ and the upper bound is $b=-1.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{-1-(-4)}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{-1}\sqrt{5}{x}^{-4}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(-4+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(-4+\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[\sqrt{5}{(-4+\frac{3i}{n})}^{-4}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-73181.html:
Question 19
?

What is ∫−4−15x−4dx expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

a
limn→∞∑i=1n[5(−2+3in)−2⋅3n]
b
limn→∞∑i=1n[5−2+5in⋅5n]
c
limn→∞∑i=1n[5(−4+3in)−4⋅3n]
d
limn→∞∑i=1n[5−4+3in⋅3n]
e
limn→∞∑i=1n[(−4+2in)−4⋅2n]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

∫abf(x)dx=limn→∞∑i=1nf(xi)⋅Δx,

where xi=a+iΔx and Δx=b−an.

In the definite integral

∫−4−15x−4dx,

the function is f(x)=5x−4, the lower bound is a=−4 and the upper bound is b=−1. So, we have

Δx=−1−(−4)n=3n.

Therefore,

∫−4−15x−4dx=limn→∞∑i=1nf(xi)⋅Δx=limn→∞∑i=1n[f(−4+i⋅3n)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑i=1n[f(−4+3in)⋅3n]=limn→∞∑i=1n[5(−4+3in)−4⋅3n].

q-346205.problem:
What is ${\int }_{2}^{5}8{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{2}^{5}8{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[8($
{{field-1}}
$)^{\,4}\cdot \frac{3}{n}]$
q-346205.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{2}^{5}8{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=8{x}^{4},$ the lower bound is $a=2$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-2}{n}=\frac{3}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{5}8{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(2+i\cdot \frac{3}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(2+\frac{3i}{n})\cdot \frac{3}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[8{(\,2+\frac{3i}{n}\,)}^{\,4}\cdot \frac{3}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$
